extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (and patent practitioners as secondary audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating Step 2B of the Alice/Mayo patent-eligibility framework: whether claim additional elements amount to an 'inventive concept' (i.e., significantly more than a judicial exception). Focuses on identifying additional elements and evaluating them individually and in combination, including improvements to computer or other technology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2B main question
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the claim recite additional elements that amount to significantly more than the judicial exception?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should first identify whether there are any additional elements (features/limitations/steps) recited in the claim beyond the judicial exception(s), then evaluate those additional elements individually and in combination to determine whether they contribute an inventive concept (i.e., amount to significantly more than the judicial exception(s)). This evaluation is made with respect to the considerations the Supreme Court has identified as relevant to the eligibility analysis (see MPEP § 2106.05(a)-(h)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify additional elements (carryover from Step 2A Prong Two)
rubrics_metrics.description: Carry over identification of the additional element(s) in the claim from Step 2A Prong Two.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should reuse their identification of additional elements from Step 2A Prong Two as the starting point for Step 2B analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate additional elements individually and in combination
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate additional elements both individually and as an ordered combination to determine whether they amount to significantly more than the judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether elements that are individually known may, when arranged in a non-conventional and non-generic combination, provide an inventive concept (e.g., BASCOM: installation of a filtering tool at a specific remote location with customizable features). The inventive-concept inquiry requires more than recognizing each claim element, by itself, was known in the art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use MPEP §2106.05(a)-(h) considerations (not a weighing test)
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply the considerations introduced in Part I.A and discussed in MPEP § 2106.05(a) through (h) to the additional elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many considerations overlap and more than one may be relevant. It is not important how elements are characterized or how many considerations apply; rather, evaluate the significance of the additional elements relative to applicant's invention and whether they encompass an inventive concept. Not all considerations will be relevant to every element or claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-evaluate prior 'insignificant extra-solution activity' findings
rubrics_metrics.description: Re-evaluate any additional element or combination of elements that was considered to be insignificant extra-solution activity per MPEP § 2106.05(g).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If re-evaluation finds that the element is unconventional or otherwise more than well-understood, routine, conventional activity in the field, this may indicate the additional element is no longer insignificant and could contribute an inventive concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine whether elements are well-understood, routine, conventional
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether any additional element or combination of elements are other than what is well-understood, routine, conventional activity in the field, or simply append well-understood, routine, conventional activities previously known to the industry, specified at a high level of generality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If elements merely append conventional computer activity at a high level of generality, they are less likely to contribute an inventive concept (see MPEP § 2106.05(d)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Outcome: claim as a whole amounts to significantly more (Pathway C) or not
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claim as a whole amounts to significantly more than the exception itself, the claim is eligible (Step 2B: YES) at Pathway C; if not, the claim is not patent-eligible (Step 2B: NO) and should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Step 2B determines whether the claim as a whole adds an inventive concept. If there are no meaningful limitations that transform the exception into a patent-eligible application, the claim is not eligible and an ineligibility rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101 should be made (see MPEP § 2106.07 for formulating rejections).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine each claim separately
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should examine each claim for eligibility separately, based on the particular elements recited therein.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims should not be judged to automatically stand or fall with similar claims in an application. One claim may be ineligible while a dependent claim that adds additional elements may be eligible because it recites elements that amount to significantly more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration: Improvements to the Functioning of a Computer or Other Technology
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether the claim 'purport(s) to improve the functioning of the computer itself' or 'any other technology or technical field.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This consideration — the search for a technological solution to a technological problem — is relevant in Step 2A Prong Two and Step 2B. Case law examples include DDR Holdings, Enfish, McRO, Visual Memory, Amdocs, and others. Determining an improvement may involve consultation of the specification to identify technical problems and unconventional technical solutions expressed in the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification must provide technical explanation of asserted improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: If it is asserted that the invention improves conventional functioning of a computer or technology, a technical explanation as to how to implement the invention should be present in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The disclosure must provide sufficient details such that one of ordinary skill in the art would recognize the claimed invention as providing an improvement. The specification need not explicitly state the improvement, but conclusory assertions without detail are insufficient. Examples: McRO relied on specification explanation; Affinity Labs failed because specification lacked details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim must reflect the disclosed improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: After the examiner determines the specification discloses an improvement, the claim must be evaluated to ensure the claim itself reflects the disclosed improvement in technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The claim must include the components or steps that provide the improvement described in the specification; it need not use explicit 'thereby' language. Consider the full scope of the claim under the broadest reasonable interpretation. Evaluate the claim 'as a whole' — as an ordered combination — and avoid oversimplifying by ignoring specific claim requirements (see cases such as Intellectual Ventures v. Symantec and McRO).

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvement must be to technology, not merely to an abstract idea or business practice
rubrics_metrics.description: An improvement in the abstract idea itself (e.g., a business or economic concept) is not an improvement in technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Improvements must be to computers or other technology/technical fields. For example, Trading Technologies held that providing more information to traders improved a business process but did not improve technology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer-specific limitation: claim scope must require computer implementation
rubrics_metrics.description: For a method claim to improve computer functionality, the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claim must be limited to computer implementation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A claim whose entire scope can be performed mentally cannot be said to improve computer technology (Synopsys). Likewise, claims covering embodiments that can be practiced verbally or by telephone cannot improve computer technology (RecogniCorp).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of improvements and non-improvements (use as evidentiary guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Court-provided examples indicate what may or may not show an improvement in computer functionality or other technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples that may show improvement (non-exhaustive): modification to hyperlink protocol (DDR Holdings); inventive distribution of functionality within a network to filter content (BASCOM); halftone rendering method; unconventional distributed network architecture; programmable memory system; detailed techniques for transmitting images; particular server structures for organized images; specific software programming/design for menus; improved virus scanning profiles; improved user interfaces; particular interfaces for 3D spreadsheets; software license restriction methods. Examples that may not be sufficient (non-exhaustive): generating restaurant menus with functionally claimed features; accelerating analysis solely via general-purpose computer speed; mere automation of manual processes; recording/transmitting/archiving digital images with conventional technology; affixing a barcode without technical details; instructions to display information without how to achieve it; improvements to information stored (not database functionality); arranging GUI information that merely assists users.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner burden and applicant response (37 CFR 1.132 evidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners are not expected to make a qualitative judgment on the merits of the asserted improvement; if the examiner concludes the disclosed invention does not improve technology, the burden shifts to applicant to provide persuasive arguments and evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant may submit a declaration under 37 CFR 1.132 to testify how one of ordinary skill in the art would interpret the disclosure as improving technology. Such evidence must establish what the specification would convey and cannot be used to supplement the specification. See MPEP § 716.09 for practice under 37 CFR 1.132 and MPEP § 2106 guidance on evaluating such submissions.
